questions.q: Why does a date column from a CSV usually need converting, even though it 'looks like' a date?
options: It typically loads as plain text (object dtype) — Pandas sees an eleven-character string, not an actual date, the same problem Lesson 13 covered
Dates are always loaded correctly by default and never need conversion
CSV files cannot contain dates at all
Only European date formats need conversion
questions.explain: A date string like '2026-01-15' is just text to Pandas until explicitly converted — the exact same object dtype issue Lesson 13 introduced, just with dates specifically.

options: Converts a text column into Pandas' actual date type (datetime64)
Converts a date column back into plain text
Deletes any column containing dates
Only works on columns already correctly typed as dates
questions.explain: to_datetime() is the specific conversion function for turning date-like text into a genuine datetime64 column that supports real date operations.

questions.q: What operations become possible only after converting a column with pd.to_datetime()?
options: Comparing dates, sorting chronologically, and calculating date differences correctly
Printing the column at all
Adding the column to a DataFrame in the first place
Nothing changes — text dates already support all date operations
questions.explain: Plain text that merely looks like a date doesn't support real chronological comparison or date math — only a true datetime64 column does.

questions.q: How do you extract just the year from a converted date column?
options: df["Order Date"].dt.year
df["Order Date"].str.year
df["Order Date"].astype(year)
Years cannot be extracted from a date column
questions.explain: The .dt accessor is the date equivalent of .str for text — .dt.year, .dt.month, and similar properties pull out individual parts of a datetime64 column.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect to the main Power BI course's DimDate table?
options: pd.to_datetime() plus .dt accessors are how you build clean, correctly-typed date structures in Python before the data ever reaches Power BI, similar in purpose to the hand-built DimDate table
There is no connection between Pandas dates and Power BI's DimDate concept
DimDate tables can only be built using DAX, never Python
pd.to_datetime() automatically creates a DimDate table inside Power BI
questions.explain: Both are about the same underlying need — genuinely typed, reliable date data — just approached from Python's side of the pipeline instead of DAX's.
